title: Gas Fees Explained: Why Sending $20 Costs $50 (And How to Fix It)
description:
Gas fees can cost more than the crypto you're trying to send. But they don't have to.

This video explains what gas fees are, why Ethereum's are so high, when they're lowest, and exactly how to avoid paying $50 to move $20.

What you'll learn:
→ What gas fees actually are in simple terms
→ Why Ethereum gas fees spike so high
→ When gas fees are at their lowest
→ How Layer 2 networks solve this problem
→ The one calculation that saves you hundreds

asr.full_text: you try to send 20 dollars worth of ethereum the app says the transaction will cost 48 in gas fees you're paying more than double to move your own money this isn't a scam it's how ethereum works but there are ways around it this video explains why gas fees exist when they're highest and exactly how to avoid getting destroyed by them gas fees are the cost of executing transactions on a blockchain. Every time you send crypto, swap tokens, or interact with a smart contract, validators have to process that action. They use computational power. They get paid for it. That payment is the gas fee. Think of it like shipping costs. The blockchain is the carrier. Your transaction is the package. Gas is what you pay to get it delivered. Ethereum can only process about 15 transactions per second. When demand is high, like during an NFT mint or a market crash when everyone's panic selling, thousands of people are trying to use those 15 slots. The network runs an auction. Whoever pays the highest gas fee gets their transaction processed first. During peak times, people bid gas fees up to US$100 or more just to get in if you're not willing to pay—your transaction sits pending for hours or fails completely. Gas fees fluctuate based on network demand, weekends are cheaper cheaper than weekdays. Late night US time is cheaper than business hours. The difference can be five times — a transaction that costs $50 on a Tuesday afternoon might cost $10 on a Sunday morning. There are tools that track gas prices in real time. Etherscan shows current gas prices. You can set alerts for when fees drop below a certain threshold. If your transaction isn't urgent, wait. OPTION 1. Use a Layer 2 network. Polygon. Arbitrum. Optimism. These are built on top of Ethereum but process transactions off the main chain. Gas fees on Polygon are fractions of a cent. You get the same security as Ethereum, but at a tiny fraction of the cost. Most major DeFi apps now support Layer Two. Option 2. Use a different blockchain entirely. Solana gas fees are under a penny. Avalanche is similarly cheap. If you are just moving coins between wallets, consider using a cheaper network. Lower fees comes with trade-offs. Layer 2 networks require you to bridge your assets, that's an extra step and an extra transaction fee upfront. Cheaper blockchains like Solana are faster and cheaper but less decentralized than Ethereum. Fewer validators means more risk of censorship or network failures. There's no perfect solution. You're choosing between cost, speed and security. Most people optimize for cost and don't realize they're giving up decentralization. Before you execute any transaction, do the math! If you're moving $50 worth of crypto and the gas fee is $40. Don't do it. Wait for fees to drop or use a layer 2. If you're moving $5,000 and the gas fee is $30, that's 0.6%. That's acceptable. The Rule Never pay a gas fee that's more than 5% of the transaction value, unless it's an emergency. This one rule will save you hundreds. Comment layer 2 if you are already using Polygon or Arbitrum, or Mainnet if you're still paying full Ethereum gas fees. Next video, I'm explaining what a rug pull actually looks like before it happens, and the warning signs that could have saved people millions. Subscribe to Unbanked, the old money had a head start. You have the internet.
